1. Finding Inflection Points with the Second Derivative

3 lecture · 2 textbook (total 5)

Inflection pointA point at which the graph of a function f changes concavity is called an inflection point of f.
Concavityf′′>0: concave up (C.U.)    f′′<0: concave down (C.D.)
Possible inflection pointIf f′′ is zero or undefined at p (f′′(p)=0 or f′′(p) DNE), then p is a possible inflection point.
Testp is an inflection point only if f′′ changes sign at p.
StepsDomain → f′ → f′′ → solve f′′=0 and f′′ DNE → sign table of f′′ → inflection point (p,f(p)).
WarningNot every point where f′′(x)=0 (or f′′ is undefined) is an inflection point (e.g. f(x)=x4 at x=0), just as not every point where f′(x)=0 is a local maximum or minimum.

2. Graphing a Function from Its Properties

1 lecture · 8 textbook (total 9)

Concavityf′′>0: concave up (C.U.)    f′′<0: concave down (C.D.)
6
Lecture Question · Ex 2
Graph a function f with the following properties: f has a critical point at x=4 and an inflection point at x=8; the value of f′ is negative to the left of 4 and positive to the right of 4; the value of f′′ is positive to the left of 8 and negative to the right of 8.
AnswerLocal min at x=4; inflection point at x=8 (C.U. before 8, C.D. after)
Full solution
x(−∞,4)(4,8)(8,∞)
f′−++
f′′++−
f↘ C.U.↗ C.U.↗ C.D.
Local minimum at x=4; inflection point at x=8.
The graph: decreasing and concave up until x=4 (lowest point), then increasing and concave up (getting steeper) until x=8, then still increasing but concave down (flattening out) after x=8.
7
Textbook Question · Problem 5
  • (a) Graph a polynomial with two local maxima and two local minima.
  • (b) What is the least number of inflection points this function must have? Label the inflection points.
Answer(b) 3
Full solution(a) For example: up to a local max, down to a local min, up to a local max, down to a local min, then up forever (a polynomial of degree 5 with positive leading coefficient).
(b) 3: between each local max and the next local min (or min and next max) the concavity must change, so there is an inflection point between each pair of neighbouring extrema: 4 extrema give at least 3 inflection points.
8
Textbook Question · Problem 6
Graph a function with only one critical point (at x=5) and one inflection point (at x=10). Label the critical point and the inflection point on your graph.
AnswerLocal min at x=5, inflection point at x=10
Full solutionFor example:
x(−∞,5)(5,10)(10,∞)
f′−++
f′′++−
f↘ C.U.↗ C.U.↗ C.D.
Decreasing and C.U. down to a local min at x=5 (the critical point), then increasing and getting steeper until x=10 (the inflection point, where it is steepest), then still increasing but flattening out (C.D.). (Same idea as lecture Ex 2.)

Textbook Question · Problem 7
Graph a function which has a critical point and an inflection point at the same place.
Answere.g. f(x)=x3 at x=0
Full solutionFor example f(x)=x3 at x=0: f′(x)=3x2, so f′(0)=0 (critical point); f′′(x)=6x changes from − to + at x=0 (inflection point). The graph is increasing, C.D. before the point, flat at the point, C.U. after it.

Textbook Question · Problem 24

Problem 24
AnswerAlways decreasing; inflection points at x1​,x2​,x3​

x<x1​(x1​,x2​)(x2​,x3​)>x3​
y′−−−−
y′′+−+−

Textbook Question · Problem 25
Sketch a possible graph of y=f(x), using the given information about the derivatives y′=f′(x) and y′′=f′′(x). Assume that the function is defined and continuous for all real x.
Problem 25
AnswerAlways increasing; inflection points at x1​ (flat) and x2​
Full solution
x<x1​(x1​,x2​)>x2​
y′+++
y′′−+−
f↗ C.D.↗ C.U.↗ C.D.
The graph is increasing everywhere. C.D. up to x1​, where it is momentarily flat (y′=0: a critical point that is neither max nor min, and an inflection point); then C.U. (getting steeper) up to x2​ (inflection point, steepest point); then C.D. (flattening) after x2​.
13
Textbook Question · Problem 26
Sketch a possible graph of y=f(x), using the given information about the derivatives y′=f′(x) and y′′=f′′(x). Assume that the function is defined and continuous for all real x.
Problem 26
AnswerLine of slope 2 for x<x1​, then increasing and concave up
Full solutionFor x<x1​: y′=2 and y′′=0, so the graph is a straight line with slope 2.
For x>x1​: y′>0 and y′′>0, so the graph is increasing and C.U.: it bends upward, getting steeper than slope 2.
So: a straight line of slope 2 up to x1​, which then curves smoothly upward (concave up) after x1​. (x1​ is not an inflection point, since y′′ does not change sign there.)
14
Textbook Question · Problem 36
Assume that the polynomial f has exactly two local maxima and one local minimum, and that these are the only critical points of f.
  • (a) Sketch a possible graph of f.
  • (b) What is the largest number of zeros f could have?
  • (c) What is the least number of zeros f could have?
  • (d) What is the least number of inflection points f could have?
  • (e) What is the smallest degree f could have?
  • (f) Find a possible formula for f(x).
Answer(b) 4   (c) 0   (d) 2   (e) 4   (f) e.g. f(x)=2x2−x4
Full solution(a) An “M” shape: rising to a local max, falling to a local min, rising to a second local max, then falling; both ends go down to −∞.
(b) 4 (if the local min is below the x-axis and both maxima are above it).
(c) 0 (if both local maxima are below the x-axis).
(d) 2 (C.D. near each max, C.U. near the min).
(e) 4 (f′ must have 3 zeros, so f′ has degree at least 3).
(f) For example f(x)=2x2−x4: f′(x)=4x−4x3=4x(1−x)(1+x), local maxima at x=±1, local min at x=0.

3. Inflection Points in Applications

1 lecture · 8 textbook (total 9)

MeaningIncreasing and C.U.: increasing faster and faster. Increasing and C.D.: increasing slower and slower. At the inflection point the quantity is changing fastest (or slowest).
15
Lecture Question · Ex 3
Figure 4.20 shows a population growing toward a limiting population, L. There is an inflection point on the graph at the point where the population reaches L/2. What is the significance of the inflection point to the population?
Figure 4.20
AnswerAt the inflection point the population is growing fastest
Full solution• At times before the inflection point, the population is increasing faster every year (increasing and C.U.: accelerating).
• At times after the inflection point the population is increasing slower every year (increasing and C.D.: decelerating).
• At the inflection point, the population is growing fastest.
16
Textbook Question · Problem 8
During a flood, the water level in a river first rose faster and faster, then rose more and more slowly until it reached its highest point, then went back down to its pre-flood level. Consider water depth as a function of time.
  • (a) Is the time of highest water level a critical point or an inflection point of this function?
  • (b) Is the time when the water first began to rise more slowly a critical point or an inflection point?
Answer(a) Critical point   (b) Inflection point
Full solution(a) A critical point (a local maximum: the depth stops rising and starts falling, so the derivative is 0).
(b) An inflection point (the depth changes from rising faster and faster, C.U., to rising more and more slowly, C.D.).
17
Textbook Question · Problem 9
When I got up in the morning I put on only a light jacket because, although the temperature was dropping, it seemed that the temperature would not go much lower. But I was wrong. Around noon a northerly wind blew up and the temperature began to drop faster and faster. The worst was around 6 pm when, fortunately, the temperature started going back up.
  • (a) When was there a critical point in the graph of temperature as a function of time?
  • (b) When was there an inflection point in the graph of temperature as a function of time?
Answer(a) 6 pm   (b) Noon; another between noon and 6 pm
Full solution(a) Around 6 pm: the temperature stopped falling and started rising (a local minimum).
(b) Around noon: the temperature changed from falling more slowly (C.U.) to falling faster and faster (C.D.). There is another inflection point between noon and 6 pm, where the fall started to slow down again (C.D. to C.U.) before the minimum at 6 pm.
18
Textbook Question · Problem 27
In 1774, Captain James Cook left 10 rabbits on a small Pacific island. The rabbit population is approximated by P(t)=1+e5.3−0.4t2000​ with t measured in years since 1774. Using a calculator or computer:
  • (a) Graph P. Does the population level off?
  • (b) Estimate when the rabbit population grew most rapidly. How large was the population at that time?
  • (c) Find the inflection point on the graph and explain its significance for the rabbit population.
  • (d) What natural causes could lead to the shape of the graph of P?
Answer(a) Yes, at 2000 rabbits   (b) 1787, 1000 rabbits   (c) 1787, 1000 rabbits
Full solution(a) The graph is an S-shaped curve rising from about 10 toward 2000. Yes, it levels off at 2000 rabbits (as t→∞, e5.3−0.4t→0, so P→2000).
(b) The population grows fastest at the inflection point, where e5.3−0.4t=1⇒5.3−0.4t=0⇒t=13.25, i.e. around 1787. Then P=1+12000​=1000 rabbits.
(c) Inflection point ≈(13.25,1000): in 1787, with 1000 rabbits (half the limiting value). Before it the population grew faster and faster (C.U.); after it, it grew more and more slowly (C.D.).
(d) At first there is plenty of food and space, so the rabbits multiply quickly; later limited food and space (and predators, disease) slow the growth, so the population levels off at what the island can support.
19
Textbook Question · Problem 28
  • (a) Water is flowing at a constant rate (i.e., constant volume per unit time) into a cylindrical container standing vertically. Sketch a graph showing the depth of water against time.
  • (b) Water is flowing at a constant rate into a cone-shaped container standing on its point. Sketch a graph showing the depth of the water against time.
Answer(a) Straight line   (b) Increasing, concave down
Full solution(a) The cylinder has the same width at every height, so the depth rises at a constant rate: the graph is a straight line through the origin (increasing, no concavity).
(b) The cone gets wider as the water rises, so the depth rises quickly at first and then more and more slowly: the graph is increasing and concave down (very steep at the start).
20
Textbook Question · Problem 29
If water is flowing at a constant rate (i.e., constant volume per unit time) into the Grecian urn in Figure 4.25, sketch a graph of the depth of the water against time. Mark on the graph the time at which the water reaches the widest point of the urn.
AnswerC.D. then C.U.; inflection point when the water reaches the widest point
Full solutionAs the urn gets wider (bottom to middle), the depth rises more and more slowly: increasing and C.D. As it gets narrower (middle to top), the depth rises faster and faster: increasing and C.U.
The time at which the water reaches the widest point is the inflection point (where the depth is rising most slowly).
21
Textbook Question · Problem 30
If water is flowing at a constant rate (i.e., constant volume per unit time) into the vase in Figure 4.26, sketch a graph of the depth of the water against time. Mark on the graph the time at which the water reaches the corner of the vase.
AnswerConcave down, then a straight line from the corner on
Full solutionBottom part: the vase gets wider as it goes up, so the depth rises more and more slowly: increasing and concave down.
Top part (straight sides, constant width): the depth rises at a constant rate: a straight line.
So the graph is a concave-down curve that becomes a straight line at the time the water reaches the corner (mark that time on the t-axis).
22
Textbook Question · Problem 31
Water flows at a constant rate into the left side of the W-shaped container in Figure 4.27. Sketch a graph of the height, H, of the water in the left side of the container as a function of time, t. The container starts empty.
AnswerRises (C.D.) to t1​, flat until 2t1​, rises slowly (C.D.) to t3​, then flat
Full solution• 0<t<t1​: the left side gets wider as it rises, so H increases more and more slowly (C.D.), until the water reaches the top of the middle divider at t1​.
• t1​<t<2t1​: the water spills into the right side, so H stays constant (horizontal line) while the right side (same size) fills.
• 2t1​<t<t3​: both sides fill together over a wide, widening region, so H increases slowly and C.D.
• t>t3​: the container is full, H is constant.
23
Textbook Question · Problem 32
The vase in Figure 4.28 is filled with water at a constant rate (i.e., constant volume per unit time).
  • (a) Graph y=f(t), the depth of the water, against time, t. Show on your graph the points at which the concavity changes.
  • (b) At what depth is y=f(t) growing most quickly? Most slowly? Estimate the ratio between the growth rates at these two depths.
Answer(a) Inflection points at y1​ and y3​   (b) Fastest at y3​, slowest at y1​; ratio about 16
Full solution(a) Bottom to y1​: the vase gets wider, so the depth rises more and more slowly (C.D.). From y1​ to y3​: the vase gets narrower, so the depth rises faster and faster (C.U.). Above y3​: wider again, so C.D. The graph is always increasing, with concavity changes (inflection points) at depths y1​ (widest point) and y3​ (narrowest point, the neck).
(b) Most quickly at y3​ (narrowest); most slowly at y1​ (widest). The growth rate is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area, i.e. to (diameter)2. From the figure the diameter at y1​ is about 4 times the diameter at y3​, so the depth grows about 42=16 times faster at y3​ than at y1​ (rough estimate from the picture).

Full solutioni. From the graph: one critical point (at x=1, f has a local max: the graph goes up then down) and one inflection point (at x=2).
ii. Df​=R because Dx​=R and De−x​=R.

f′+−
f↗↘
At x=1, f has a local max: f(1)=e−1≈0.37.
f′′(x)=(−e−x)(1−x)+e−x(−1)=−e−x(1−x+1)=ex−(2−x)​
f′′(x)=0⇒2−x=0⇒x=2∈Df​    f′′(x) DNE: ex=0, no solution.
x(−∞,2)(2,∞)
f′′−+

5. Inflection Points from a Graph of f, f′ or f″

3 lecture · 5 textbook (total 8)

From the graph of f′Inflection points of f are where f′ changes from increasing to decreasing or vice versa (local max or min of f′).
From the graph of f″Inflection points of f are where f′′ changes sign (the graph of f′′ crosses the x-axis, not just touches it).

Textbook Question · Problem 1
Indicate the approximate locations of all inflection points. How many inflection points are there?
Problem 1
AnswerThree
Full solutionThree: one between the first local max and the local min, one between that local min and the second local max, and one between the second local max and the last local min (where the curve changes between C.D. and C.U.).

Textbook Question · Problem 35
Indicate on Figure 4.29 approximately where the inflection points of f(x) are if the graph shows
  • (a) The function f(x)
  • (b) The derivative f′(x)
  • (c) The second derivative f′′(x)
Answer(a) 3 points   (b) 4 points   (c) 2 points
Full solution(a) Where the concavity of the graph changes: one between each local max and the next local min (or min and next max): 3 points.
(b) At the local maxima and minima of f′ (where f′ changes from increasing to decreasing or back): 4 points.
(c) Where f′′ changes sign (crosses the x-axis): 2 points. The point where the graph only touches the axis is not an inflection point.
